messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The accident happened on a rainy Tuesday evening in March, two years ago. Samir was driving home from a long day of audits, his briefcase full of tax returns on the passenger seat, when a drunk driver ran a red light and T-boned his sedan at an intersection. The smell of alcohol from the other driver’s breath, mixed with the acrid scent of deployed airbags and hot metal, was the first thing Samir registered before the pain in his ribs and the sight of blood on his hands. He spent three days in the hospital with a fractured sternum and whiplash, but the physical wounds healed faster than anything else.

In the months that followed, Samir found himself unable to drive. The mere sight of a car that resembled his own—a silver four-door sedan of the same make and model—sent a cold spike of fear through his chest. He began taking the bus to work, but even that was not safe. Whenever the bus passed an intersection, or when he heard a sudden loud sound—a car backfiring, a construction worker’s hammer, a door slamming—his heart would hammer and he would find himself scanning the road for oncoming headlights. He became hypervigilant on the street, always watching, always waiting, convinced that another collision was just around the corner. The world felt dangerous in a way it never had before, and Samir had come to believe that he could not trust himself to navigate it. He told his therapist that he felt no longer capable of doing the things that defined him—driving his son to soccer practice, meeting clients across town, even just running a simple errand. He had lost his confidence, and with it, the sense that he would ever feel normal emotions again. What frightened him most was the certainty that something inside him was permanently broken.

To cope, Samir developed a set of strategies that made sense to him at the time. He stopped eating regular meals, skipping breakfast and lunch because the act of sitting down to eat felt too exposed, too vulnerable. He would come home from work and immediately retreat to his phone, spending hours scrolling through social media or playing mindless games, anything to avoid the intrusive crash imagery that surfaced whenever he closed his eyes. The most significant change was his complete avoidance of driving. He would not get behind the wheel, and he refused to be a passenger in anyone else’s car, even his own brother’s. This meant he could no longer visit his parents, who lived forty minutes away, and he had to ask his ex-wife to handle all drop-offs and pick-ups for their seven-year-old son. The shame of this dependency only deepened his belief that he could not rely on himself.

The smell of alcohol became a particular torment. One evening, walking home from the bus stop, Samir passed a bar and caught a whiff of beer on the night air. Instantly, he was back in the car, the smell of the drunk driver’s breath filling his nostrils, his ribs aching with phantom pain. He froze on the sidewalk, his pulse roaring in his ears, before turning and walking a full mile out of his way to avoid that block ever again. He began to notice the smell everywhere—on a stranger’s breath in the grocery store, at a neighbor’s barbecue, even faintly on his own hands after using hand sanitizer. Each time, the threat response surged, a full-body alarm that left him trembling and exhausted. And each time, he retreated further into his routines: more screen time, less food, narrower paths through the city.

Over time, the cycle tightened. The more he avoided, the more he came to believe that he was incapable of handling the world. The more he hypervigilantly scanned for threats, the more triggers he found—a car that looked like his, a sudden sound, a whiff of alcohol. By the time he walked into a therapist’s office, he had lost twelve pounds, his social circle had shrunk to almost nothing, and he had been written up at work for repeatedly refusing to attend field audits that required him to ride with a colleague. He was terrified that he would never be the father, the professional, the person he used to be. But what finally brought him through the door was a simple, desperate hope: that maybe, if he could learn to trust himself again, he might one day drive his son to school.
